newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore parliament agrees to electoral changes.
newsitem.headline: Singapore parliament agrees to electoral changes.

text.p: Singapore's parliament passed bills on Monday to change electoral laws despite opposition protests that the moves would weaken their election chances.
The legislation had also caused concern in some quarters that it might jeopardise ethnic minority representation.
The government said the changes were aimed at devolving more authority and responsibility to local communities and their members of parliament (MPs).
The changes, coming ahead of general elections due by April 1997, allow a multi-member group representation constituency (GRC) to elect a maximum of six MPs, up from four currently.

The legislation was passed with only the parliament's four opposition MPs voting against. They said the election rules were changed at the last minute to weaken their poll chances and demanded a referendum on the matter.

Defending the moves, Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong said: "Our system evolves from our own experience of multiracialism and to develop teamwork. We want to move to our own form of selecting our political representatives."
Goh's People's Action Party (PAP) took 77 of 81 parliamentary seats in the last general elections in 1991.
In the GRCs, votes are cast for slates rather than single candidates. The team winning the most votes takes all seats.
Each team must include at least one minority member, as one basis for GRCs is to ensure minimum minority representation in parliament, as well as to form town councils to run public housing estates.

"Town Councils were set up to give more authority and responsibility to residents to manage their own estates," Goh said. "I intend to devolve still more authority to the local communities, by setting up Community Development Councils."
Goh said increasing the number of MPs in a GRC was electorally neutral. He said the opposition had a chance of winning all the seats in GRCs if they put up good teams.

But opposition MP Ling How Dong said the moves would deprive voters of the right to pick individual candidates, forcing them to vote for slates. "The amendments are more to strengthen the ruling party and entrench their continuous rule," he said.
Political analysts have said the PAP could benefit by having well-known ministers lead its teams, and the opposition could have problems finding enough candidates for six-person slates.
The proposal to raise the number of MPs in a GRC had also sparked a debate, echoed by some MPs, over whether it would reduce minority ethnic representation.
Goh said the PAP would run more than one minority candidate in the larger GRCs, and future changes could be made to write more guarantees for minority representation into law.
There are now 17 minority MPs from 15 GRCs and Goh said this was more than the minimum six prescribed under existing law.

Chinese form the majority of Singapore's three million people. Minorities include Malays at 14.1 percent of the population, Indians at 7.1 percent, and other races -- which include a mix of Eurasians and Arabs -- at 1.1 percent.
